cross_references.label: CMIA — Standard Civil Damages
cross_references.note: §56.36(a) incorporates §56.35's full damages framework (nominal, exemplary, actual, punitive, attorney fees) for persons who negligently or intentionally release medical information. §56.36 then adds criminal penalties and triple damages on top.

cross_references.label: CMIA — Authorized Disclosures
cross_references.note: §56.36 attaches to violations of §56.10 (unauthorized disclosures). The 'false pretenses' provision of §56.36(b)(1) specifically targets those who falsely claim a §56.10(b)/(c) exception or present fraudulent authorizations.

cross_references.label: CMIA Definitions
cross_references.note: §56.36(d) incorporates §56.05's definition of 'medical information.' The same definition governs both the disclosure rules (§56.10) and the criminal penalty track (§56.36).

cross_references.label: Extortion — Related Criminal Framework
cross_references.note: Where medical information is used to extort money or action from a patient, §518 extortion charges may apply alongside §56.36 criminal penalties. The two criminal tracks are not mutually exclusive.

cross_references.label: Federal Civil Rights — State Actor Liability
cross_references.note: State actors (probation officers, court investigators, law enforcement) who obtain medical records under §56.36's false-pretenses framework are simultaneously acting under color of law. §1983 claims are available where the unauthorized access was conducted by a state actor or under state authority.

cross_references.label: Federal PHI Rules
cross_references.note: HIPAA violations involving unauthorized access to PHI may occur simultaneously with §56.36 violations. State and federal enforcement tracks operate in parallel; CMIA generally provides stronger individual remedies.

cross_references.label: CMIA — Patient Access to Own Records
cross_references.note: §56.20 gives the patient the right to obtain their own records. §56.36(b)(1) criminalizes others obtaining those records under false pretenses. The two provisions protect the same records from opposite directions.
